title: Curative in vivo genome writing beyond the liver

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a way to make durable, disease-changing edits directly inside a person's blood-forming stem cells and at least one solid tissue outside the liver, such as skeletal muscle or the central nervous system. An editor would reach the relevant cells, alter their DNA and produce lasting therapeutic benefit without collecting cells for external editing or using transplantation-level marrow conditioning. “Curative” describes the intended clinical outcome; it is not an outcome established for this proposed platform.

The central challenge combines delivery with editing. A molecular editor must reach enough of the right cells and perform a useful genetic change safely. The supplied lipid-nanoparticle review describes human liver-directed editing and animal progress outside the liver, while identifying safe, efficient delivery as a major bottleneck. Its explanation of liver accumulation concerns intravenously administered lipid nanoparticles; it does not establish that every delivery method has the same distribution.

The proposed platform would demonstrate useful breadth through blood stem cells and a solid non-liver tissue. It need not use the same formulation or administration route for both applications. Local delivery could qualify if it produced the required therapeutic coverage and durability. Reaching every tissue systemically, editing every cell or correcting every mutation is outside this definition.

significance.text: A successful platform could extend durable genetic treatment to selected diseases whose affected cells are difficult to edit inside the body. The technical starting points are meaningful but separate: human liver-directed editing, disease-changing ex vivo blood-stem-cell editing and preclinical extrahepatic delivery. Combining therapeutic extrahepatic access with durable editing would connect these capabilities and could support additional disease-specific treatments.

For a successfully demonstrated blood-stem-cell treatment, direct in vivo editing without conditioning could remove the need for stem-cell collection, external manufacturing and myeloablative preparation. CASGEVY illustrates the burdens that this could avoid: its established ex vivo treatment requires these steps, and its label identifies infertility as a risk associated with myeloablative conditioning. Avoiding that regimen would be a substantial clinical advance, although the in vivo treatment would still need its own safety evaluation.

Conditional impact assessment: one-time cures for additional hemoglobin disorders, muscle diseases or nervous-system diseases would remain separate achievements. Each would require a compatible edit, adequate coverage of the relevant cells, durable benefit and acceptable safety. Correcting a molecular defect may prevent further injury without reversing damage that has already occurred. Demonstration in two tissue settings would therefore establish a broader treatment approach, not a general cure for genetic disease.

Scope limitation: this capability would not automatically enable body-wide correction of complex polygenic risk, eradicate cancer, reverse aging or clear persistent viral reservoirs. Related editing tools might contribute to those goals, but delivery alone would not resolve their distinct biological barriers. The supplied evidence also does not justify a broad claim that gene addition using AAV has failed across the relevant diseases.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is safe, efficient and tissue-selective delivery coupled to therapeutically effective genome editing in humans outside the liver. The supplied review explains that most intravenously administered lipid nanoparticles accumulate in the liver, including through interactions involving apolipoprotein E and hepatocyte receptors. Extrahepatic delivery must overcome this distribution bias and deliver the necessary editing components to the intended cells in a functional form. Animal extrahepatic editing is evidence of progress, but it does not establish durable therapeutic benefit in humans.

Engineering synthesis: success requires more than detecting an edit in a tissue sample. Delivery must cover the disease-relevant cell population, and the editor must make a useful change at sufficient frequency. For blood disorders, editing short-lived circulating cells would not substitute for durable modification of the stem cells that replenish them. For muscle or central nervous system disease, the required distribution and target-cell types would depend on the disease; a small accessible region might be insufficient for a widespread disorder.

Safety and durability synthesis: the treatment must control unintended genetic changes, harmful editing of other cell types, delivery-related toxicity and immune responses. Edited stem cells must retain useful long-term blood-forming function without harmful clonal expansion. In solid tissues, benefit must persist in the relevant cells and remain adequate as cells turn over or disease progresses. The acceptable balance of editing efficiency and risk must be determined for each disease rather than inferred from a platform-wide percentage.

Removing transplantation-level conditioning is a distinct part of the blood-stem-cell challenge. CASGEVY requires mobilization and collection of the patient's stem cells, ex vivo manufacturing and full myeloablative conditioning before infusion. This establishes the regimen for that product; it does not prove that every possible ex vivo hematopoietic editing approach biologically requires marrow ablation.

current_state.text: The supplied review, identified as published online on May 28, 2025, with a January 2026 issue date, documents human liver-directed editing studies and preclinical extrahepatic work, including blood stem cells, lung and muscle. These are different levels of demonstration: animal delivery or editing does not establish a human cure. According to the supplied evidence review, the retained article text includes the main sections but is truncated within the references, and its figures were not inspected.

For nexiguran ziclumeran, the earlier research describes a 2024 phase 1 ATTR cardiomyopathy study in which one infusion lowered serum transthyretin by about 90% at 12 months in 36 patients, without a control group. Those quantitative and design details remain provisional here: the source index contains no captured copy of the cited NEJM report, so the supplied evidence review could not verify them. The earlier research also recorded only limited confirmation of access beyond the displayed page. Even if confirmed, serum-protein reduction would demonstrate liver-directed biological activity rather than establish extrahepatic editing or, by itself, a cure.

The earlier research describes a May 2025 report of a patient-specific lipid-nanoparticle base editor given to one infant with hepatic CPS1 deficiency, with improved metabolic control over seven weeks and a need for longer safety and efficacy follow-up. It identifies hepatocytes as the delivery target. These details are retained as an attributed account, not independently confirmed findings: the first research pass reported abstract-level access, and no article artifact was retained for the supplied evidence review. A short single-patient liver-directed result would not establish durable correction outside the liver.

CASGEVY provides a documented clinical comparison. The supplied label, identified in the research as updated July 7, 2026, describes exagamglogene autotemcel as an autologous product made from collected stem cells edited outside the body. It requires full myeloablative conditioning and specifies infusion between 48 hours and seven days after the last conditioning dose. Its clinical results establish disease-changing ex vivo editing for specific hemoglobin disorders. The supplied evidence review reports that the retained label text was complete and untruncated.

Unverified research detail: the earlier research identifies a 2026 NEJM BEACON report on risto-cel, described as an autologous base-edited hematopoietic product that raised fetal hemoglobin in sickle cell disease. No supporting report text or source URL was supplied for that assertion, so its dated findings cannot be established from this record. As described in the research, the product is an ex vivo stem-cell treatment and would not demonstrate the proposed in vivo capability.

The evidence package does not establish whether the complete proposed capability remained undemonstrated through November 1, 2026. Its freshness record is empty, so the earlier statement that curative in-body editing of muscle, brain or unconditioned blood stem cells “was not found” cannot serve as a comprehensive absence claim. Missing article captures limit verification; they do not show that the reported results are false.

A PDF attached to the review's source entry was identified by the supplied evidence review as a 2023 VERVE-101 conference presentation. It is a separate document from the lipid-nanoparticle review and the missing NEJM reports, and cannot verify their specific results. The source index also records PDF extraction warnings, which further constrain reliance on that extracted material.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: a common platform should produce durable, disease-changing genome editing in humans in both blood-forming stem cells without transplantation-level conditioning and at least one solid non-liver tissue, such as skeletal muscle or the central nervous system. Different disease-specific editors, formulations or local administration routes could be used, provided the shared platform contribution is clear. A liver-only demonstration, including a successful single-patient treatment, would not satisfy this proposed scope.
completion_criteria.label: Durable human editing spans hematopoietic stem cells and non-liver tissue

completion_criteria.text: Proposed efficacy criteria: each application should demonstrate clinical benefit alongside molecular evidence that the intended cells were edited. Editing levels should be justified against disease-specific therapeutic requirements; where such thresholds are unknown, editing percentage alone should not substitute for functional or clinical outcomes. For blood stem cells, evidence should distinguish persistent stem-cell modification from transient editing of downstream cells. For solid tissues, it should establish sufficient coverage of the cells responsible for the disease.
completion_criteria.label: Clinical benefit accompanies therapeutically sufficient editing of disease-relevant cells

completion_criteria.text: Proposed durability and safety criteria: benefit should persist for years with follow-up suited to the disease and edited cell population. Protocols should prospectively define permitted conditioning, clinical endpoints, follow-up duration and acceptable genetic, tissue and immune risks. Assessment should include unintended editing, delivery toxicity and, where relevant, long-term blood-cell function and clonal behavior. These are proposed evaluation requirements, not established consensus standards or completed results.
completion_criteria.label: Benefit persists for years with prospectively defined safety criteria

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: convincing evidence should extend beyond an isolated responder, with reproducible manufacturing and outcomes across appropriately selected patients and clinical settings. Studies should state the mutations, tissues, disease stages, administration routes and patient characteristics tested. Finite trials can demonstrate useful breadth and practical reliability; they cannot establish literal universality, and neither 100% editing nor access to every tissue is required.
completion_criteria.label: Manufacturing and clinical outcomes reproduce across patients and settings

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: CLM-01, Programmable antigen-specific immune tolerance, could intersect with managing responses to an editor or delivery vehicle, but selective immune tolerance is a separate therapeutic capability. CLM-02, Clearance of persistent viral reservoirs that force lifelong therapy, could use some of the same delivery tools, yet requires reaching and eliminating or disabling persistent infection. CLM-10, Vaccines that elicit broad protection against hypervariable viruses, addresses protective immunity against viral diversity rather than correction of inherited DNA.

Roster-based synthesis: CLM-03, Arrest and recovery of function in symptomatic Alzheimer’s disease, and CLM-04, Restoration of adult human central nervous system circuitry after injury, overlap with the challenge of reaching relevant brain cells. A successful central nervous system edit would not itself establish arrest of Alzheimer’s disease, recovery of lost function or reconstruction of injured circuits. CLM-12, Selective, durable control of pathological chronic pain, could potentially use targeted genetic interventions, but its defining outcome is selective pain control rather than broad extrahepatic genome editing.

Roster-based synthesis: CLM-06, Therapeutic remuscularization of the adult human heart, and CLM-15, Restoration of nephron number in the adult human kidney, concern rebuilding functional tissue. Editing might address a contributing genetic defect or support a regenerative intervention, but correction of existing cells does not establish creation of new myocardium or nephrons. CLM-05, Durable organ xenotransplantation at clinical scale, and CLM-11, Implantable human-scale organs assembled outside the body, concern replacement organs; genetic engineering may contribute to them, while CLM-09 targets cells inside the recipient.

Roster-based synthesis: CLM-07, Reproducible eradication of metastatic carcinoma, and CLM-08, Safe multi-tissue reversal of human biological aging, could overlap with editing and delivery technologies. Their outcomes require control of cancer or reversal of aging across relevant biological systems; therapeutic correction of selected genetic diseases would establish neither. CLM-13, Population screening that shifts unscreened lethal cancers to a curable stage, concerns earlier detection and treatment timing, with little direct overlap in its defining capability.

Roster-based synthesis: CLM-14, A shelf-stable oxygen carrier that can replace donor red cells in hemorrhage, shares a broad connection to blood medicine but addresses immediate oxygen transport during bleeding. Editing blood-forming stem cells addresses durable production of therapeutically useful blood cells and would not provide an emergency substitute for donor red cells. These remain distinct innovations.

The infant CPS1 case's treatment details, seven-week outcomes, hepatocyte targeting and subsequent durability require confirmation from the uncaptured report and later follow-up.
The identity, publication details and clinical findings of the claimed 2026 risto-cel BEACON report remain unverified in the supplied evidence.
The empty freshness record prevents determining whether later human demonstrations met the proposed scope by November 1, 2026.
A future evaluation protocol must define the common platform, permissible conditioning, disease-specific efficacy and safety thresholds, required patient numbers and follow-up duration.
The reviewed lipid-nanoparticle extraction is truncated within its references and excludes figure inspection, limiting assessment of details beyond the retained main text.

brief.title: Lasting genetic treatments beyond the liver
possible: People with selected inherited diseases could receive lasting treatment by having DNA changed directly inside their bodies. Treatment would reach blood-forming stem cells—the cells that continually replenish blood—and a solid tissue outside the liver, such as muscle or brain.
For blood disorders, this could avoid collecting cells, editing them in a laboratory and giving intensive treatment to clear the bone marrow before returning them.
why: This could extend durable genetic treatment to diseases whose affected cells are difficult to reach. Patients with some blood, muscle or nervous-system diseases could gain treatments that address their genetic cause.
Avoiding intensive marrow preparation could also remove a major burden of current blood-stem-cell treatment, including its associated infertility risk.

shown: Human DNA editing has reached the liver. CASGEVY has established disease-changing treatment for selected inherited blood disorders by editing collected stem cells outside the body.

Fan Wu and colleagues describe animal progress in reaching blood-forming stem cells, lung and muscle. These advances remain separate from a shared approach that delivers lasting human benefit across the required tissues.
missing: Editors still need to reach enough disease-relevant cells outside the liver and make changes that produce lasting human benefit.
Blood-forming stem cells need lasting edits inside the body without transplantation-level marrow preparation.
Treatment needs to control unintended DNA changes, delivery toxicity, immune reactions and harmful expansion of edited cells.

milestones.label: Lasting human treatment reaches blood stem cells and another tissue
milestones.explanation: A shared approach would have to deliver lasting, disease-changing edits in blood-forming stem cells without intensive marrow preparation and a solid tissue outside the liver. This would establish its breadth.

milestones.label: Editing the relevant cells produces clinical benefit
milestones.explanation: Each application would have to link patient benefit to sufficient editing of the cells responsible for disease. This would distinguish useful treatment from merely detecting DNA changes.

milestones.label: Benefit lasts for years within defined safety limits
milestones.explanation: Benefit would have to persist for years under safety criteria set before treatment, covering genetic changes, tissue damage and immune effects. This would establish whether lasting editing delivers lasting value.

milestones.label: Manufacturing and patient outcomes prove reproducible
milestones.explanation: Manufacturing and clinical outcomes would have to repeat across suitable patients and clinical settings, with the tested scope clearly defined. This would establish reliability beyond an isolated responder.

uncertain: The amount and distribution of editing needed for benefit will depend on the disease.
Correcting a genetic defect may prevent further injury without reversing existing damage.
How much follow-up, how many patients and what shared technology would establish a reliable platform remain open questions.

page.title: In vivo genome editing beyond the liver
page.definition: The goal is FDA-licensed treatment that changes DNA inside a patient's own cells, with clinical benefit established in two settings. One is the blood-forming stem cells that replenish the blood throughout life. Treatment there must avoid cell collection, transplantation and myeloablative conditioning, the chemotherapy used to deplete marrow before transplantation. The other is at least one solid tissue outside the liver, such as the retina. A different treatment can qualify in each setting.

goal.need: Millions with sickle cell disease and other blood disorders lack access to gene therapy. Six patients in a sickle cell trial could not receive CASGEVY because too few stem cells were collected. All 44 recipients had severely low neutrophil and platelet counts after conditioning and infusion. Editing stem cells in place could remove the need to collect and process each patient's cells and spare patients the infertility risk of marrow-depleting chemotherapy. In inherited retinal degeneration, the prospect is better vision if enough editor reaches the affected cells safely.

completion.title: FDA licenses in vivo editing of blood stem cells and at least one solid tissue outside the liver.
completion.criterion: FDA has licensed one or more genome-editing treatments covering both blood-forming stem cells and at least one solid extrahepatic tissue. Editors act inside the patient; the stem-cell regimen requires no cell collection, transplantation or myeloablative conditioning. Each indication has established clinical benefit over the disease-specific follow-up accepted by FDA. Accelerated approval based only on a surrogate qualifies after clinical benefit is verified. Different editors, carriers and administration routes may qualify.
completion.set_by: Atlas operational definition combining the two tissue settings with FDA product-specific licensing requirements.
completion.basis: FDA licenses each biological product under 21 CFR 601.4. Under 21 CFR 601.41, FDA may approve a product on a surrogate endpoint and require further study to verify clinical benefit. The Atlas requires established benefit in each of the two settings. The NIH delivery challenge and NHLBI stem-cell programme define separate goals and specify no joint licensing test or common follow-up period.

milestones.criterion: The editor produces the intended DNA alteration in the disease-relevant human cell type in culture, in tissue or in an organoid. FDA recommends assessing activity in the target cell type and specifies no common editing percentage.

milestones.title: An in vivo editor has preclinical activity and safety evidence supporting a human starting dose.

milestones.set_by: FDA, Preclinical Assessment of Investigational Cellular and Gene Therapy Products, section III.A, and Human Gene Therapy Products Incorporating Human Genome Editing, section IV.

milestones.title: A person receives an in vivo genome editor under an effective FDA IND.
milestones.criterion: At least one participant receives the editor under an effective FDA investigational new drug application (IND), with applicable ethics approval and informed consent. The IND goes into effect 30 days after FDA receives it unless FDA imposes a clinical hold, or earlier if FDA notifies the sponsor that the investigation may begin.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 21 CFR 312.40: administration to human subjects requires an effective IND.
milestones.threshold_quote: An investigator may not administer an investigational new drug to human subjects until the IND goes into effect

milestones.title: An in vivo editor establishes clinical effectiveness in adequate and well-controlled investigations.
milestones.criterion: Adequate and well-controlled clinical investigations establish effectiveness for the indication using disease-appropriate endpoints and follow-up. If the sponsor relies on one adequate and well-controlled investigation, confirmatory evidence must support it.
milestones.set_by: FDA’s statutory substantial-evidence standard, described in its notice of 24 June 2026; the accompanying revised guidance remains a draft.
milestones.threshold_quote: sponsors relying on one adequate and well-controlled clinical investigation to establish substantial evidence of effectiveness must provide confirmatory evidence.

milestones.title: An editor administered in vivo produces the intended biological response in a relevant animal model.
milestones.criterion: Administration to a relevant animal model produces the intended editing-related biological response in the target-cell setting. A species-specific surrogate editor can be used when sequence differences make the clinical editor uninformative and the surrogate's biological relevance is established.
milestones.set_by: FDA, Human Gene Therapy Products Incorporating Human Genome Editing, section IV, recommendations for in vivo proof-of-concept studies.
milestones.threshold_quote: should demonstrate a biological response to the human GE product

milestones.title: A clinical study shows preliminary evidence of effectiveness for the target indication.
milestones.criterion: An investigation in patients with the target condition reports an outcome suggesting effectiveness for that indication. The measure and follow-up depend on the disease. Dosing and safety observations alone do not establish this stage.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 21 CFR 312.21(c), description of the evidence preceding expanded phase 3 investigations.
milestones.threshold_quote: after preliminary evidence suggesting effectiveness of the drug has been obtained

not_found: No published human blood-stem-cell editing result meeting the stated in vivo regimen was identified.
No regulator or professional-society statement was found judging therapeutic in vivo editing in these two settings unachievable or unworthy of pursuit.

results.finding: In 37 CASGEVY-treated sickle cell patients assessed at month 6, a mean 86.1% of alleles in bone marrow CD34+ cells carried the intended edit.
results.detail: The percentage measures alleles in marrow CD34+ cells after infusion. The label provides no corresponding percentage for the manufactured cells before infusion.

results.finding: Among 31 efficacy-evaluable sickle cell patients treated with CASGEVY, 93.5% achieved the 12-month severe crisis-free endpoint.
results.detail: These clinical outcomes followed transplantation of autologous stem cells edited ex vivo and myeloablative conditioning.
results.quote: Of the 31 efficacy-evaluable patients, the primary efficacy outcome of VF12 response was achieved in 29 of 31 (93.5%, 98% one sided CI: 77.9%, 100.0%) patients with a median duration VOC-free of 22.2 months.

results.finding: In the younger pediatric sickle cell trial, 100% of 8 efficacy-evaluable CASGEVY recipients achieved the 12-month severe crisis-free endpoint.
results.detail: The trial regimen included apheresis, ex vivo editing, myeloablative conditioning and autologous stem-cell transplantation.
results.quote: Of the 8 efficacy-evaluable patients, the primary efficacy outcome of VF12 was achieved in all 8 patients (100%), with a median (min, max) duration VOC free of 17.5 (13.2, 21.3) months.

definition = "The goal is FDA-licensed treatment that changes DNA inside a patient's own cells, with clinical benefit established in two settings. One is the blood-forming stem cells that replenish the blood throughout life. Treatment there must avoid cell collection, transplantation and myeloablative conditioning, the chemotherapy used to deplete marrow before transplantation. The other is at least one solid tissue outside the liver, such as the retina. A different treatment can qualify in each setting.". Reason: The present tense makes licensing sound accomplished, and the retinal example clarifies that local administration can qualify.

goal.need = "Millions with sickle cell disease and other blood disorders lack access to gene therapy. Six patients in a sickle cell trial could not receive CASGEVY because too few stem cells were collected. All 44 recipients had severely low neutrophil and platelet counts after conditioning and infusion. Editing stem cells in place could remove the need to collect and process each patient's cells and spare patients the infertility risk of marrow-depleting chemotherapy. In inherited retinal degeneration, the prospect is better vision if enough editor reaches the affected cells safely.". Reason: The trial's collection failures quantify a barrier that editing cells more efficiently after collection cannot solve, and vision gives the solid-tissue goal a concrete patient outcome.

add statement by Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, address to the American Association for the Advancement of Science, 2020: "a single injection using vectors that target and edit blood-forming cells in the bone marrow". Reason: The 2020 address identifies editing blood-forming cells in the marrow as an explicit sickle cell goal of the foundation's collaboration with NIH.

edit completion: basis = "FDA licenses each biological product under 21 CFR 601.4. Under 21 CFR 601.41, FDA may approve a product on a surrogate endpoint and require further study to verify clinical benefit. The Atlas requires established benefit in each of the two settings. The NIH delivery challenge and NHLBI stem-cell programme define separate goals and specify no joint licensing test or common follow-up period."; refs = [2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 20]. Reason: The licensing basis omits the regulation that distinguishes an effect on a surrogate endpoint from verified clinical benefit.

edit m1: criterion = "The editor produces the intended DNA alteration in the disease-relevant human cell type in culture, in tissue or in an organoid. FDA recommends assessing activity in the target cell type and specifies no common editing percentage.". Reason: The donor count and editing percentage are findings from one experiment and could be mistaken for the cell-activity threshold.

add milestone after m1: "An editor administered in vivo produces the intended biological response in a relevant animal model.". Reason: Editing human cells in culture leaves delivery untested, while a biological response in a living model can be demonstrated before a human starting dose is justified.

edit m2: criterion = "Product-specific evidence on biological activity, distribution in the body and toxicity supports the proposed human starting dose and the feasibility and reasonable safety of the planned route of administration."; set_by = "FDA, Preclinical Assessment of Investigational Cellular and Gene Therapy Products, section III.A, and Human Gene Therapy Products Incorporating Human Genome Editing, section IV."; threshold_quote = "Selection of potential starting dose level, dose-escalation schedule, and dosing regimen for clinical trials."; threshold_ref = 9. Reason: The mouse transplantation result addresses biological activity, while the cited FDA objective concerns selection of the human starting dose.

edit m3: criterion = "At least one participant receives the editor under an effective FDA investigational new drug application (IND), with applicable ethics approval and informed consent. The IND goes into effect 30 days after FDA receives it unless FDA imposes a clinical hold, or earlier if FDA notifies the sponsor that the investigation may begin.". Reason: The retinal and muscle trial findings obscure the legal test of actual dosing under an effective investigational new drug application.

add milestone after m3: "A clinical study shows preliminary evidence of effectiveness for the target indication.". Reason: The sequence jumps from first dosing to established effectiveness and leaves no place for preliminary evidence of improved function in patients.

edit m4: criterion = "Adequate and well-controlled clinical investigations establish effectiveness for the indication using disease-appropriate endpoints and follow-up. If the sponsor relies on one adequate and well-controlled investigation, confirmatory evidence must support it.". Reason: The visual-acuity change and descriptive confidence intervals belong to the retinal trial, while the effectiveness standard applies separately to every indication.
remove not found 2. Reason: Full reports of the liver-directed ATTR study and the infant CPS1 treatment are accessible in references 22 and 23.
remove not found 1. Reason: The muscle paper's abstract omits the denominator, but the sponsor's publication notice in reference 24 confirms four participants treated at two dose levels.

add not found: "No regulator or professional-society statement was found judging therapeutic in vivo editing in these two settings unachievable or unworthy of pursuit.". Reason: Safety concerns about particular products do not establish institutional opposition to the therapeutic goal.
